claims.text: The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has a single-phase FCC structure.
Adding a few atomic percent Mo to CoCrFeNi will produce a continuous, adherent MoO3 tribofilm during elevated-temperature sliding.
At elevated temperatures, Mo segregates to the sliding surface.
Surface-segregated Mo preferentially oxidizes to form MoO3.
MoO3 is a layered oxide with self-lubricating properties.
A MoO3 tribofilm reduces interfacial shear resistance.
Reduced interfacial shear resistance lowers the coefficient of friction.
Formation of the MoO3 tribofilm reduces wear rate.
Oxidation is minimal at lower test temperatures.
At lower temperatures, adding a few atomic percent Mo leaves the alloy microstructure similar to that of Mo-free CoCrFeNi.
At lower temperatures, adding Mo leaves tribological performance similar to that of Mo-free CoCrFeNi.
Mo-alloyed CoCrFeNi will have a lower coefficient of friction than Mo-free CoCrFeNi at temperatures approaching 800 °C.
Mo-alloyed CoCrFeNi will have a lower wear rate than Mo-free CoCrFeNi at temperatures approaching 800 °C.
Mo-alloyed CoCrFeNi will maintain room-temperature friction and wear performance comparable to Mo-free CoCrFeNi.
Mo addition will reduce friction and wear throughout the full room-temperature-to-800 °C range.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says Mo reduces friction and wear across the full temperature range, whereas the mechanism and predicted outcome state that lower-temperature or room-temperature performance remains merely similar or comparable to the baseline.
